title: [D5 Tools] Budget guards enforced at the tool boundary
summary: `helena.budgets` is the budget guard: `RunBudget` is one ledger per agent run carrying the four dimensions from `AgentRequest.budgets` and what has been spent of each, and both `helena.agents.assess` and `helena.tools.ProviderTool.lookup` now take it keyword-only with no default and charge the same object — so the wall clock covers the whole run including provider waits, steps and live queries are refused inside the dispatch rather than discouraged in a prompt, and a spent dimension is a typed `ToolRefusal` carrying `budget_exhausted`. The values are loaded from `config/policy.toml` beside the thresholds, the live-query count is derived from the retrieval allowance and the slowest configured provider rate rather than configured, and `budgets.degraded` turns a truncated `normal` analyst verdict into `unknown` with the exhaustion explicit, through the contract's own validation.
assumption_validated: That `concept/07`'s four dimensions can be enforced where they are actually spent without a supervisor, a second store or a contract change — and the increment validated it with two corrections worth carrying. (1) SPENT IS NOT TRUNCATED. The first shape marked the token dimension exhausted whenever the remainder reached zero, which degrades a run that spent its last token on the answer it returned — a good verdict rewritten to `unknown` for using its budget efficiently, which is `concept/07`'s unassessable/assessed collapse arriving from the accounting side. A dimension is now exhausted only when the run asked for more and was refused, and every guard records its own. (2) THE LIVE-QUERY BUDGET CANNOT HONESTLY BE CONFIGURED. `concept/07` requires it and the wall clock to be 'set against each other', so it is derived — floor(retrieval_seconds x slowest rate / 60) — and the loader refuses four ways the pair can contradict itself. Measured consequence of the ordering in the dispatch: a run whose live-query quota is spent still gets answers from the cache, because the quota is charged after the cache read, and that is a test.
makes_buildable: Task 39 (the analyst tool loop) gets the object the loop is bounded by and the two calls it makes: `budget = RunBudget.of(request)` once, then `tool.lookup(arguments, scope=..., budget=budget)` per turn and `assess(request, ..., budget=budget)` per model call, with `degraded(outcome, budget)` at the end. It needs no budget arithmetic of its own and cannot accidentally get a fresh clock. Task 37 (send policy and disclosure) has the refusal vocabulary it extends — `REFUSAL_REASONS` is now three — and the place its check goes is the same dispatch, after the budget and before the cache read. Task 38 (the live adapter) has the number it must pace itself to (`config/policy.toml`'s `[rate_limits]`) and the guard that catches it when it does not: provider waits are on the run's clock. Task 43 (assessment persistence) gets `RunBudget.cost(retries=...)` as the row's budgets-consumed, latency, tokens and cache-hit-versus-live-query columns, and owes the two things named in the escalations: the monetary column with the price table it is derived from, and a `budgets_version` if it wants to record which budget policy governed a run.

verification.detail: 1289 passed in 294.74s, no skips, engine and broker up (bin/env.sh sourced). New: tests/test_budgets.py 44 tests (the ledger over an injected clock, the degrade rule, the policy loader and the derivation), 9 in tests/test_tools.py driving the real dispatch against the migrated engine and the real ThreatFox extract, 2 in tests/test_agents.py against the local stub endpoint. No new SQL — the cache tables from 0017 are what the tool tests execute against, unchanged.

escalations.detail: A DERIVED MONETARY COST IS NOT BUILT, and the task's last step asks for it. Three reasons and each is a rule: (a) deriving it needs a per-model price table and no price table exists in this repository, so a figure would be an invented external fact — the class of error `concept/instruction.md` §0 is about; (b) a monetary field on `helena.contracts.v1.Cost` is a change to the agent contract, which §3 makes an escalation; (c) `concept/06` says the cost is 'derived and recorded PER ASSESSMENT', which is a stored column, and no assessment table exists (deferred to task 43). What is built is the half that holds: nothing caps cost separately, and `Cost` carries the two token counts the derivation consumes. Task 43 should add the column, the price table and the version of that table it records.

`helena/budgets.py` IS A NEW TOP-LEVEL MODULE, and `tests/test_package_layout.py` asserts the module set exactly, so this is a deliberate edit rather than a file appearing. `concept/03`'s component table has a row for 'policy and budget guards'; the layout test read it as 'the deterministic code in orchestration', and that is not possible — the ledger is charged by `helena.agents` AND `helena.tools`, and `orchestration` is the module that will import both, so a ledger defined there is an import cycle. The policy half of the same row is already outside `orchestration` for its own reason (a frozen rule version needs a versioned package). Recorded in docs/decisions/0026 §8 and in the layout test's own comment. No dependency, store, egress channel or contract field was added.

`helena.agents.assess` NOW TAKES A REQUIRED `budget` ARGUMENT, which changed 21 call sites in tests/test_agents.py (through one `assessed()` wrapper) and one in `helena.triage.run`. It is required rather than defaulted on purpose: a ledger built inside `assess` would restart the wall clock and the token count on every turn of an analyst tool loop, which is the unbounded run the dimension exists to bound, and `assess` also refuses a ledger whose limits are not the request's. Flagged because it is a public-ish seam a later increment might otherwise assume optional.

invariant_conflicts.conflict: The task's step 'record ... derived monetary cost on the assessment' versus `concept/instruction.md` §3 (a contract field is an escalation) and §0 (check the artifact, not the page — there is no price table to check). Resolved in favour of the invariants: the cost is not capped, the tokens are measured, and the money is not claimed. See the first escalation.

The task's step 'emit a `budget_exhausted` gap and degrade the verdict' versus `concept/07`'s triage asymmetry: triage has no `unknown` root (`taxonomy.v1.TRIAGE_ROOTS` is `normal`/`suspicious`), so a truncated triage verdict has nothing to degrade TO. Resolved by the concept: a context triage could not assess is a typed failure, which `assess` already produces with the gap on it, and `degraded` raises `BudgetError` rather than inventing a third triage label. The degrade path is the analyst's.

deferred: PACING CALLS TO THE CONFIGURED RATE. `config/policy.toml`'s `[rate_limits]` is read for the derivation and nothing sleeps between calls, so the rate the tool layer 'holds itself to' is not yet a rate it enforces in time. The live adapter (task 38) is where a throttle belongs — it is the only thing that knows a request left the process — and the wall-clock budget already charges the wait when it happens. Stated in the module docstring, the config file and README rather than implied.

A MEASURED PROVIDER RATE LIMIT. `[rate_limits] threatfox = 4` is a self-imposed ceiling, not a measurement: abuse.ch publishes fair-use terms rather than a number, and measuring one would mean deliberately exceeding it against a live service. `concept/07`'s own 'a few lookups per minute' is the shape it comes from, and it must be lowered the moment a provider states less.

EVERY NUMBER IN `[budgets.*]` IS A CANDIDATE. No per-run token consumption has been measured, no provider latency distribution exists, and `concept/08` still lists the numeric budget values as open. What is demonstrated is that they are loaded from the file, enforced at the boundary, and changeable without touching code — the same standing the 0.80 threshold and `config/agents.toml`'s 3 have.

`budgets_version`. Deliberately NOT added to `config/policy.toml`: `thresholds_version` exists because an `Escalation` records it, and nothing records a budget version — no assessment row exists and `Budgets` has no version field. A key nothing reads is what the rest of that file refuses. Task 43 adds it with the column that reads it.

SERVING AN EXPIRED RECORD WHEN THE LIVE-QUERY BUDGET IS SPENT. The call is refused instead, and the choice is argued in ADR-0026 §3: the stale fallback exists because the PROVIDER did not answer, and letting a budget decide what the evidence is would make two runs differing only in budget differ in what they cite. If a later increment wants the other behaviour it is a change to this decision, not an optimisation.

NOTHING STORES A `Cost`, so 'budgets consumed, latency and tokens are recorded on the assessment' is a ready shape and not a property that holds. `RunBudget.cost()` produces the record; task 43 stores it.

NO AGENT HAS BEEN BUDGETED THROUGH A TOOL LOOP, because no analyst loop exists (task 39). Every dimension is enforced and tested at the boundary it is enforced at, and nothing has yet driven all four in one run of a real agent.

`degraded` HAS NO CALLER IN THE TREE. `helena.triage.run` deliberately does not call it — a triage `AgentResult` can never come back from a ledger that refused something (the only guards on that path are `check_tokens`, which ends the run with a failure, and the clock, which is `timed_out`), so calling it there would be dead code that could only ever raise. The analyst runner is its caller.
lessons: SPENT IS NOT TRUNCATED, and the difference decides whether a good verdict survives. A dimension whose remainder reached zero is not the same as a run that asked for more and was refused: the first is a run that finished, the second is the one `concept/07` degrades to `unknown`. `RunBudget.exhausted` records refusals only, and `record_tokens` (which reports spending that already happened) marks nothing. Collapsing the two turns 'used its budget efficiently' into 'unassessable'.

THE ORDER OF THE CHARGES IN THE DISPATCH IS THE DESIGN. A step and the clock before anything else, so an unbounded loop cannot be bought with malformed calls and a finished run does not do work nobody can use; the live query AFTER the cache read, so a hit costs no quota and a run out of quota can still read what it already fetched. That last one is a measured consequence and a test, not an intention.

ONE LEDGER PER RUN, PASSED IN, NEVER BUILT INSIDE. `assess` used to compute its own deadline from `request.budgets`, which is correct for a single exchange and wrong for a loop: every turn would get the full wall clock again. The fix is a required argument, and the check that makes it safe is `assess` refusing a ledger whose limits are not the request's.

`model_copy` SKIPS `model_post_init`, so it cannot be used to rewrite a contract object that has rules. `degraded` re-validates through `model_validate_json(json.dumps(...))` — the shape `assess` already uses, because the contracts are `strict=True` and python mode refuses the list a dump produces where a tuple is declared. Written the short way, the degrade could have produced exactly the `normal`-with-a-budget_exhausted-gap outcome `concept/07` forbids, and the contract would never have seen it.

A DERIVED NUMBER NEEDS ITS INPUTS KEPT. `BudgetPolicy` carries `rate_limits` and `retrieval_seconds` beside the four dimensions so the test recomputes the live-query budget from them rather than comparing it with a number written down twice — which is the same rule as the duplicated-version-constant one, applied to arithmetic.

TWO LOADERS OVER ONE CONFIG FILE NEED ONE KEY LIST. `policy.thresholds()` refuses a top-level key nothing reads, so adding `[budgets]` to `config/policy.toml` would have made it refuse to start. `helena.policy` now names both `THRESHOLD_KEYS` and `BUDGET_KEYS` (it owns the path), `helena.budgets` imports them, and a test asserts the committed file loads under both.
failed_approaches: Marking the token dimension exhausted inside `record_tokens` (i.e. whenever the remainder hit zero). It made `degraded` unsafe for a successful run: a triage `normal` that validated on its last token would either be rewritten to a root triage does not have, or crash the caller. Rejected before it was committed and replaced by `check_tokens`, which is the guard the loop already needed.

Putting the ledger in `helena/orchestration.py`, where `tests/test_package_layout.py`'s comment said the budget guards live. It is an import cycle: `orchestration` will import `helena.agents` and `helena.tools`, and both charge the ledger. Do not move it back without resolving that — see docs/decisions/0026 §8.

Configuring `live_queries` directly in `config/policy.toml`. It reads as the obvious shape and it is the one `concept/07` explicitly rules out ('the wall-clock budget and the live-query budget have to be set against each other, not independently'): two independent numbers means one of them never binds, and which one is a property of a rate limit nobody wrote down. The loader now refuses a file that states it.

`pgrep -f "pytest -q"` to check on the background suite. It matches this session's own argv, because the task prompt contains that string — the same trap session-memory records for `pkill -f 'bin/risingwave'`. It reports the agent process, not pytest, and a `-9` would have killed the session. Use the background task's output file, or `pgrep -x`.
next_session_should_know: Task 37 is the disclosure record and the send policy, and the dispatch it edits now has a budget in front of it. SEVEN THINGS TO CARRY. (1) THE CALL IS `tool.lookup(arguments, scope=RunScope.of(request), budget=RunBudget.of(request), now=...)`. `budget` is keyword-only with no default, exactly like `scope`, and for the same reason — there is no argument a model could put one in and no way for a caller to omit one and still get a lookup. `helena.agents.assess` takes the same object under the same rules. (2) THE CHARGE ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING AND YOUR CHECK GOES AFTER IT: a step and the clock first (so a malformed call still costs a turn of the loop), then argument validation, then the entity-type check, then the cache read, then the live query. A send-policy refusal belongs between validation and the cache read, and it costs a step and no live query — `REFUSAL_REASONS` is now `(malformed_arguments, entity_type_not_covered, budget_exhausted)` and `tools.BUDGET_EXHAUSTED` IS `contract.BUDGET_EXHAUSTED`, imported rather than respelled. (3) A CACHE HIT ANSWERS AFTER THE QUOTA IS SPENT. That is deliberate and tested: the live query is charged after the cache read. Do not move a check that could refuse the call to before the cache read unless you mean 'this run may not read what it already fetched' — which is what the wall-clock check does mean. (4) `exhausted` MEANS REFUSED, NOT SPENT. `RunBudget.gap()` returns the `budget_exhausted` gap only when the run asked for more of something and could not have it; a run that spent its last token on the answer it returned is a run that finished. `degraded(outcome, budget)` is the only place code rewrites a classification, it re-validates through the contract, and it RAISES for a triage `normal` because triage has no `unknown` root. (5) THE VALUES ARE IN `config/policy.toml` NOW, IN TWO NEW TABLES, AND `live_queries` IS NOT A KEY — it is derived from `retrieval_seconds` and the slowest `[rate_limits]` entry, and the loader refuses a pair that contradicts itself. `helena.policy.THRESHOLD_KEYS` and `BUDGET_KEYS` are why both loaders still start on that file; add a key to neither loader's set and it will be refused, which is the intended behaviour. (6) `[rate_limits] threatfox = 4` IS SELF-IMPOSED AND NOT MEASURED, and NOTHING PACES CALLS TO IT. If task 38 confirms a published limit, that number moves and the derived live-query budget moves with it; if you add a throttle, the wall-clock budget is already charging the wait. (7) THE FULL SUITE IS 1 289 TESTS IN ~295 s ON THIS MACHINE, NO SKIPS. `tests/test_budgets.py` needs no engine (the ledger is arithmetic over an injected `Clock`); the budget tests in `tests/test_tools.py` do, because that whole module is integration, and `ledger()`/`driven()` there are the helpers to reuse.
